https://www.wsbtv.com/news/local/atlanta.text: Atlanta Business owner says midtown Atlanta construction forced salon to close, sparked rent dispute By Ashli Lincoln, WSB-TV July 21, 2026 at 8:40 pm EDT By Ashli Lincoln, WSB-TV July 21, 2026 at 8:40 pm EDT ATLANTA — A midtown Atlanta business owner says years of road closures tied to a major construction project cut off customer access to her nail salon, ultimately forcing the business to close. [DOWNLOAD: Free WSB-TV News app for alerts as news breaks ] Tajunsar Diallo, the former owner of Soaked & Polish nail salon at the corner of 12th Street NW and Spring Street, says she believes construction related to the development resulted in her being evicted from the property. The area has been under construction for about three years as developers build a mixed-use high-rise tower that is expected to be the tallest building constructed in Atlanta since 1992. The tower is located right across the street from Diallo’s salon. Portions of 12th Street between West Peachtree and Spring Street have remained closed during the project. Diallo said her business survived challenges including the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2024 Midtown Atlanta water main breaks. “We was out of business for like a week and a half. I still pay my rent. I didn’t ask for any help,” Diallo said. She said the construction proved to be a much greater obstacle. “We was all blindsided by this whole project,” she said. TRENDING STORIES: Pan Am Clipper Endeavor found; plane missing for 74 years Metro Atlanta superior court judge facing official charges of misconduct from state commission Malcolm-Jamal Warner’s widow sues his mother over pre-nup According to Diallo, the road and sidewalk closures made it difficult for customers to reach her salon, dramatically reducing revenue. “I can bring between $50,000 to $60,000 a month. I was only bringing in $20,000, $25,000 to $30,000,” she said. Diallo said she and other tenants asked property management for financial relief because of the construction’s impact. In a letter reviewed by Channel 2 Action News , property management acknowledged that “construction has impacted not only the community but the city,” but said a rent concession was not available. Diallo said she later learned a neighboring tenant received an offer for a 12-month rent reduction. “I was not evicted because I was a negligent owner. This project itself basically put me out of business,” she said. [SIGN UP: WSB-TV Daily Headlines Newsletter ] Court records show the property’s owners sued Diallo in 2025, seeking nearly $10,000 in unpaid rent. Diallo said declining business made it difficult to keep up with rent payments. She is representing herself in the case, which remains pending. Channel 2 Action News contacted the attorney representing the property’s management company for comment but did not receive a response. Diallo said she now drives for Uber while continuing to fight the lawsuit. “I didn’t see the writing on the wall until it was too late,” she said. ©2026 Cox Media Group 0 View Comments Most Read Attacks on water supply: Cybercriminals target at least 2 Georgia systems Missing couple found dead in crash; puppy alive in car 4 people shot, 1 dead inside Atlanta apartment ‘Walking houseplant’ looks right at security camera after car stolen Attorney fights murder charge for mom in 1-year-old son’s hot car death

https://www.adgully.com/post/19829/polan.text: Poland urges European Commission to fine Meta €250 million over fraudulent ads Poland has formally requested the European Commission to impose a €250 million ($291.3 million) fine on Meta, accusing the social media giant of failing to curb fraudulent advertisements across its platforms. Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski announced the move, stating that repeated warnings and reports submitted by Polish cybersecurity authorities yielded an inadequate response from the company. The minister cited findings from CERT Polska, Poland’s national cybersecurity incident response team, which tested 122 reported advertisements identified as scams. According to Gawkowski, Meta refused to remove 106 of the flagged ads—representing 86.8% of the sample—while taking down only 10 and leaving six without any response. Urging immediate intervention by the European Commission, Gawkowski called on Meta to deploy robust tools to eliminate false advertising, financial scams, and the promotion of illegal applications. Photograph: Maskot/Getty Images Students University students say procrastination is biggest threat to their academic performance More than half of US students surveyed said the problem damaged their ability to do academic work, study finds Richard Adams Education editor Thu 8 Oct 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Procrastination is the biggest problem that can harm students’ academic performance at university, according to a study of more than 65,000 young people who placed it above issues such as ADHD, anxiety or financial worries. The study found that nearly half of the students surveyed named procrastination as the thing damaging their ability to do academic work, more than twice the number who named depression, while the same proportion said procrastination caused them significant distress above any other problems including family pressures or bullying. Itamar Shatz, the author of the study and an affiliated lecturer at the University of Cambridge, said that while he expected the survey of US students would show that they experienced harm from procrastination, he was surprised by how strongly it affected them. ‘Lonely, terrifying and scary’: 70% of students in UK university halls feel isolated, poll shows Read more Shatz said: “Pretty much all of us procrastinate but it’s not a huge impediment for all of us. For the people that it is, it can be huge. It’s not just something we occasionally run into but, as we can see in these findings, it can be a major obstacle. “It’s an obstacle that can interfere with academic success, with success in the workplace, it can cause issues in relationships, it can cause stress, it can cause health issues and stop us reaching out for help.” The study, published in the journal Plos One , also suggests that procrastination could be a factor in a “vicious cycle” that can cause or exaggerate other issues such as stress. “An example of such a feedback loop is a student procrastinating on a task, which causes them to feel stressed, which interferes with their sleep, which causes them to procrastinate on the task further,” the study said. Fuschia Sirois, a psychology professor at Durham University and a co-editor-in-chief of the British Journal of Health Psychology, who was not involved in the study, said: “The salience of procrastination in students’ lives and its harms has been a topic of research for almost 30 years, with the first studies on the impact of procrastination on health and wellbeing conducted in the late 1990s and early 2000s. So this is an issue for which there is an established evidence base that clearly highlights the negative impact of procrastination on students’ lives. “This descriptive study with a large sample provides some additional insights into the relative impact of procrastination with respect to its range of harms. But it is just a snapshot, so limits the conclusions we can draw.” Sirois said myths about procrastination “being a character flaw” have persisted despite the existing research. Revealed: the university courses students regret – and those they don’t Read more “People procrastinate to avoid the difficult emotions associated with a task, which affords them short-term mood repair. But in the long run the feelings of guilt, shame and stress from procrastinating catch up to them and take a toll on health and wellbeing,” she said. Shatz, who has recently published a guide to overcoming procrastination, said that procrastination should not be compared with laziness, because procrastinators can often be highly motivated to tackle a task only to be derailed by other distractions such as perfectionism or burn-out. Universities should be aware that many of their students are likely to be hampered by procrastination. “They should understand that procrastination isn’t just a time management flaw that they can fix with a flyer, but it is one of the biggest obstacles that students face and needs to be treated with positive interventions. The good thing is that research shows that interventions can help,” Shatz said.
